summary: Source-anchored research for Vague attribution and weasel wording. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: The same guide says LLMs present views from one or two sources as widely held, mention multiple 'reviewers' while citing only one person, and imply lists are non-exhaustive when the sources do not. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

Scope limit: the manual says such phrases are not automatically weasel words. They can stand in a lead or topic sentence when the article body or rest of the paragraph supplies attribution, and can be used for views properly attributed to a reliable source. (medium confidence)

Wikipedia's 'Signs of AI writing' has a section on vague attributions and overgeneralization of opinions: chatbots attribute opinions to vague authorities via weasel wording, with phrases like 'Industry reports', 'Observers have cited', 'Experts argue', 'Some critics argue', 'several sources/publications'. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

Wikipedia's Manual of Style defines weasel wording as vague attribution that dresses a statement in authority with no substantial basis; its examples include 'some people say', 'many scholars state', 'it is believed', 'experts declare', 'it is often reported'. (high confidence)

A 2009 Wikipedia study grouped weasel wording into numerically vague expressions, passive voice that avoids accountability ('it is said'), and weakening adverbs ('often', 'probably'). (low confidence)

An interuniversity style guide (UPC) gives the same fix outside Wikipedia: 'Student registrations have been observed to be increasing' becomes 'Student registrations have been increasing'; a straightforward statement beats a vague attribution. (medium confidence)
